b: Our man in San Francisco Ned Raggett hears about joint single 'Cross Whisper', birds as harbinger of the beyond and the problem of long patch cables... Portraits by Travis Shinn

Martin Gore’s experience across nearly half a century of music making, whether in or out of Depeche Mode, covers a lot of ground. But even he didn’t guess that his latest release, ‘Cross Whisper’, a collaborative single with lyricist Cliff Damavandi, would get past a creative roadblock courtesy of Johnnie Lee – his 10-year-old daughter – and her primary school timetable.

“I called Cliff over and said, ‘Look, have a listen. I don’t think it’s really working,'” Gore says on a joint Zoom call with Damavandi. “Then Cliff said, ‘What about if we got somebody to whisper the vocals?’ I said, ‘Well, my daughter’s off school today. I could go and ask her.’ Things just fell into place. Had she not been home from school, maybe it would never have happened!”

It is indeed Johnnie Lee’s voice, almost a spectral presence asking questions before a full slow electronic crunch of a beat kicks in, which provides the entry point into ‘Cross Whisper’. It’s a song that both showcases Gore’s very distinct style of electronic composition but also feels like something a little different in turn via its slightly fractured and layered lyric, not to mention Gore and Lee’s vocal contributions interweaving as much as other elements of the arrangement do.

Gore’s repeated invocation of a “little black bird” speaks to the origins of the track. The subject matter sprang from a discussion at a vinyl listening club, held in his longtime home town of Santa Barbara. Club cofounder Damavandi initially met Gore through mutual friends during COVID, and a friendship developed after their kids formed a learning / play pod during the worst of lockdown. He had his own musical experiences to bring to bear on the song in turn.

“I’ve done a lot of abstract art, mixed media,” says Damavandi, “but my primary business is real estate development. Think three-dimensional art, houses, buildings, resorts, that type of stuff. But I’ve been writing lyrics probably since I was nine, and I’m a big vinyl collection guy. I was a DJ for a little bit in 1992 to 1994 in Hollywood, but never had the chance to fully absorb myself in it.”

As Gore described it, birds have made appearances in his life whenever someone close to him has died. That in turn led Damavandi to work on creating a lyric from Gore’s story, following a general process he describes as “more of a feeling than cerebral.” This all led to the vivid mix of questions, mantras, avian imagery and reflections on “the great void” and life within it that defines the song.

“The words create the melodies,” Damavandi elaborates, “so I start humming and thinking, but I’d never say it’s fully set. I really feel this is describing an experience as an example with Martin or, in other cases, taking stories. I’ve traveled a lot in my life, so experiences are a big part. What drives my words is, ‘How do I capture this moment?'”

It’s part of an intriguing change in recent years for Gore when it comes to lyrical collaboration. After having spent most of his songwriting career working on his own words, a number of songs on the last Depeche album, Memento Mori, were cowrites with Richard Butler of Psychedelic Furs. “I think it was actually in 2020 when Richard reached out to me and said, ‘We should write some songs.'” remembers Gore. “They turned out very much in the vein, I thought, of Depeche Mode, so I had to ask him and he was like, ‘Yeah, of course.’ So that was good, took a bit of pressure off me for the rest of the writing!”

In terms of music, there is a sense of dark relentlessness and a delicate but clearly present beauty, which are equally matched to the lyrics. It was a creative process that Gore describes as “just as I go and as we went, really. The beats were very heavy and even the bass was very heavy, but then we had to work that around the whispering. So it was a question of getting these really high intensity moments, then dropping it down so that you could hear the whispers. That happened a lot during the making of this song.”

Unlike Gore’s past solo efforts, the final release ‘Cross Whisper’ does not have extra original songs. The additional tracks consist of a variety of remixes from other artists, following a long established pattern for Gore in and out of Depeche. Standouts include Pye Corner Audio’s slinky steady punch of a rework and ANNA’s brisk high speed pulse, with lyrical elements flitting amid the rush.

“Mute do suggest some people,” says Gore when asked how remixers end up working on any of his projects, “but I think that virtually all the people we ended up using this time, I think the ideas came from us. When we were trying to come up with names, I said, ‘I know ANNA’s done a lot for me, and it seems like going back over past glories or whatever, but she always delivers and she always does something interesting.’ So fortunately, we reached out and her schedule allowed her to do it.”

Damavandi adds, “I think the driving premise was we wanted dance music. We wanted people moving to it, and so we would always pick the players that we thought could deliver that faster beat, and the tempo was important.”

The pair say there are no plans to do any more music together beyond this, but it’s clearly an experience both have enjoyed, and whatever the future holds, it may involve more experiments in Gore’s now famed modular synth room in his home – an Aladdin’s cave of blinking modules. When asked how his setup currently works, he mentions keeping cases on the floor and patching from there as opposed to his older wall setup: “I can just get a module out and put it in a case if I want to use something in particular. I don’t need the super huge cables but they still have to be pretty big.”
“I could attest to that,” Damavandi interjects. “I tripped over a few of them when you were making this!”
“Yeah,” laughs Gore, “the studio is definitely a trip hazard, perhaps a death hazard!”
MG x CD + JL= – ‘Cross Whisper’ is out on 15 January 2027
